findings.title: Unauthenticated zlib decompression bomb in URLSafeSerializer.load_payload
findings.description:
Entry: src/itsdangerous/serializer.py:392 (Serializer._loads_unsafe_impl feeds the attacker's unverified payload to load_payload; the same decode is shown in docs/serializer.rst:58 and exercised by tests/test_itsdangerous/test_serializer.py:78).
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller who can submit a token string to an application that inspects tampered payloads with URLSafeSerializer or URLSafeTimedSerializer (loads_unsafe, load_unsafe, TimedSerializer.loads_unsafe, or the documented load_payload(e.payload) pattern), crossing the boundary where payload bytes are expanded without a valid signature and without any size bound.
Path: the token is split by Signer.unsign (signer.py:244-256); when the signature check fails, the value before the last separator is attached to BadSignature.payload; serializer.py:392 passes it to URLSafeSerializerMixin.load_payload (url_safe.py:23); because it starts with b"." (url_safe.py:32-34) it is base64-decoded and url_safe.py:46 calls zlib.decompress(json) with the default max_length=0, materializing the entire decompressed output in memory before json.loads runs.
Why nothing stops it: no length cap exists on the token in loads/loads_unsafe and no cap exists on the decompressed size; the try/except Exception at url_safe.py:47-51 only converts failures (including MemoryError) into BadPayload after the allocation was attempted; the token needs no valid signature on this path, so the attacker fully controls the compressed bytes.
Impact: deflate expands up to about 1000:1, so one compact unauthenticated request (a ~1 MB token) makes the server allocate roughly a gigabyte, and a handful of concurrent requests exhaust memory and can OOM-kill the worker, taking the whole application down.
Fix: bound the decompression output, e.g. use zlib.decompressobj() and decompress(data, max_length) with a configurable cap (rejecting anything larger as BadPayload), or pass max_length to zlib.decompress and treat the truncated result as an error; also bound the accepted payload/token length before decoding.
